sources.news_title: Republican Drops Painfully Simple Theory About Trump's Pathological Fibs
sources.text:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) thinks he has an explanation for President Donald Trump’s stubborn aversion to the facts.
During a Sunday appearance on “Meet the Press,” the senator shared a theory about why he thinks the president is doubling down on his claim that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was damaged by vandals and not crumbling apart due to a rushed renovation job, as his own Justice Department admitted in a Friday court filing.
“The president says it was caused by vandals. I don’t know if he really believes that or it’s part of his political messaging or he’s just thinking out loud,” Kennedy mused to host Kristen Welker.
“He grows anxious when he has an unexpressed thought,” the senator went on.
After indicting Olympian David Hearn with vandalism charges that could carry a 10-year sentence, the DOJ decided to reverse course in light of documents from the Interior Department and a visual inspection of the monument.
“Given all of this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt,” U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro wrote in court documents moving to formally dismiss the case.
Trump, however, rebuffed Pirro‘s determination, writing he “100%” disagreed with the decision in a Truth Social post. He did not provide any additional evidence to support his claim.
Following the news, Hearn’s legal team said the move to dismiss his case couldn’t be described as complete justice, noting how it could not “erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong.”
“The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim,” they said, adding that the administration owes Hearn an apology.

sources.news_title: Seriously? “I Don’t Know Whether He Really Believes That” – Senator John Kennedy Says Trump is “Anxious”, Defends Jeanine Pirro Dropping Charges Against David Hearn * The Gateway Pundit * by Jordan Conradson
sources.text:
Senator John Kennedy (R-LA) appeared to trash Trump over charges that were recently dropped against the accused reflecting pool vandal, David Hearn, during a Sunday appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press.
Kennedy suggested Trump has grown “anxious” and that he may not really believe Hearn committed a crime, while defending Jeanine Pirro’s decision to drop the charges.
Over a dozen people have been arrested or cited for their suspected role in the vandalism, but the most notable arrest was that of former Olympian David Hearn.
A grand jury in far-left DC returned an indictment of the three-time Olympic canoeist for his alleged vandalism of the reflecting pool last month. Hearn faced up to ten years in prison after a grand jury in the DC Superior Court returned the indictment.
When he was arrested in June, local independent journalist Emily Miller appeared to catch his arrest on camera. She shared the clip on X, saying he was vandalizing the pool and tried to impede workers cleaning the pool by “grabb[ing] the hose that female National Park Service workers were using to clear the algae.” It is unclear if this claim was even presented to the grand jury that returned an indictment.
However, as The Gateway Pundit reported, the Justice Department on Friday dropped the charges against Hearn. US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, who previously accused Hearn of “violently and forcefully” ripping up the sealant, claimed on Friday that “flawed installation by the contractor” was responsible for the damage.
Trump lashed out at Pirro on Saturday morning, slamming her for dismissing the case.
Trump went on to share a four-minute-long surveillance video of alleged vandals writing on Truth Social, "Look for yourselves at the VANDALISM that took place at The Reflecting Pool. The material is being cut with a knife or a box cutter, for all to see!" Previously, the US Park Police shared part of this footage and requested help from the public in identifying the suspect as part of a destruction of government property investigation.

Asked about the David Hearn case and whether the reversal could "undercut the public's faith in the Justice Department," Senator Kennedy described the case as a "multiple vehicle pileup," suggesting President Trump is being dishonest.
"Let me start with the president. The president says it was caused by vandals. I don't know whether he really believes that, or it's part of his political messaging, or he's just thinking out loud," he said.
"You and I both know the president well. He exists loudly, and he grows anxious when he has an unexpressed thought. I'm not saying he doesn't really believe it. I just don't know."
On Pirro, he noted that the stakes are higher in a court of law and suggested that she would need to lie in order to secure a conviction. "You can't lie to a federal judge. If she can't prove her case, she was right to pull back because if you fool around with a federal judge, you will find out," he said.
He then suggested that there was never any evidence against Hearn, saying, "I don't know why she filed the suit without having without doing a full investigation. She says she relied on the Department of Interior, but she was smart to pull it back."

Foghorn Leghorn: Exclude Rioters From Slush Fund
sources.text:
NBC News reports:
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that he would not provide the Trump administration with a “blank check” for the proposed “anti-weaponization” fund and that rioters who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, should not be allowed to benefit from it.
Kennedy appeared open to supporting a bill to enshrine the $1.776 billion fund into law, which has emerged as a primary sticking point holding up the nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general.
Asked whether anyone who attacked law enforcement or stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6 should be able to receive taxpayer money from the fund, Kennedy said he would “take them off the table.” “It’s too emotional of an issue, and it’s too important of an issue,” he said.
Read the full article. Kennedy also says that he “wouldn’t bet my house” on Blanche ever being confirmed.

sources.news_title: John Kennedy: Would not give Trump ‘a blank check’ on anti-weaponization fund legislation
Trump is giving his supporters taxpayer money whether anyone likes it or not
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s economic policies are so clearly based on benefiting those with proximity to the president that critics have denounced them with terms like “crony capitalism” and “communism of pelf.” Now a series of commentators observed that one of the most controversial manifestations of these policies — his $1.776 billion slush fund to Trump supporters who claim they were persecuted by the government — is likely to proceed despite it being ruled illegal by a judge and fiercely opposed even by many members of Trump’s own Republican Party. 
“The $1.8 billion slush fund that would help these insurrectionists would be coming from a bigger pot called the Judgment Fund, right?” explained lawyer and legal commentator Katie Phang on MS NOW. She had previously described how Trump’s pick for attorney general, acting attorney general Todd Blanche, has so far not been able to be confirmed because Republican lawmakers like Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas oppose his refusal to promise the slush fund is dead.
“The Judgment Fund is used to pay out settlements and verdicts and judgments that stem from Federal Tort Claims Act litigation, or claims made against the federal government,” Phang explained. “But those FTCA claims get vetted, ostensibly by a legitimate Department of Justice review. So when you think about the idea that there would be somebody who would legitimately, credibly gatekeep these claims — yeah, that's what the FTCA was designed to do. The government screws up, they've got to pay it out.”
She added, “That's a totally separate thing, right? The real corruption here is the initiation of the lawsuit and its genesis. Trump wanted to give cover to create the slush fund for the insurrectionists and for his buddies whom he wanted to be able to pay out money to, including people like Michael Caputo, Steve Bannon, and Michael Flynn. So he created this lawsuit with the whole charade of it. And when a federal judge busted him on it, he essentially said, ‘Oh well, I can just do this the way I want to through a bill.’ That's not going to work either, because as Tillis said, you're not going to get the support from Republicans to get it across the finish line.”
Earlier in the same interview, MS NOW political analyst Steve Benen observed that Trump’s slush fund is so politically toxic, Republican lawmakers — despite normally deferring to Trump’s wishes — have been uncharacteristically bold in taking a stand against it.
“I think it hasn't really been fully explored yet, because when you look back at the context of the Senate right now, John Cornyn and Thom Tillis are taking the lead on this,” Benen said. “But according to both of them, they're not alone. They say that they're representing a variety of Republican senators who share the same concerns they do about the Blanche nomination. And in fact, in recent days, we've seen a lot of evidence of that. We saw [Republican Sen.] Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, whose term in Congress is also soon ending, saying he has concerns. We've seen Alaska's [Republican Sen.] Lisa Murkowski stepping up and saying, ‘You know what? Maybe Blanche's confirmation isn't going to happen.’”
Benen added, “And so really, this resistance isn't limited to two people stepping up. We're seeing broader concern among GOP senators saying maybe Blanche's nomination is no longer a sure thing.”
The slush fund in question was created because Trump sued the IRS due to an independent contractor leaking his tax returns in 2018, thereby showing he had not paid income taxes for multiple years and had a string of previously-undisclosed business failures. Even though no one has ever been compensated for this issue and has instead merely received apologies, Trump sued the IRS for $10 billion. When a judge overseeing the case questioned the lawsuit’s legality — noting that Trump both controls the IRS he is using and the Justice Department that is supposed to defend the IRS — the president and Blanche rushed to “settle” the suit for $1.776 billion, to be dispensed to Trump supporters and Trump-affiliated institutions, as well as a pledge to spare Trump and his family all future audits.
Judge Kathleen M. Williams quickly overturned the settlement, saying that it was an illegal form of self-dealing and could not be ethically implemented. By contrast, one of the potential beneficiaries of the slush fund — former 2016 Trump campaign worker and lawyer Sam Nunberg — told AlterNet in June that he believes the so-called “anti-weaponization fund” is justified.
“If it's a political witch hunt, yeah. I think there should be some kind of compensation fund for it, and I don't care what party the people are from,” Nunberg argued.

sources.news_title: Sen. John Kennedy says he’d exclude Jan. 6 rioters from ‘anti-weaponization’ fund legislation
sources.text:
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that he would not provide the Trump administration with a “blank check” for the proposed “anti-weaponization” fund and that rioters who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, should not be allowed to benefit from it.
Kennedy appeared open to supporting a bill to enshrine the $1.776 billion fund into law, which has emerged as a primary sticking point holding up the nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general.
Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina have said they would only support Blanche if the Justice Department alters the conditions of President Donald Trump’s settlement with the IRS over his leaked tax returns and provides assurances that the fund is officially dead.
The settlement had established the “anti-weaponization” fund, which the Justice Department backed off from after bipartisan pushback, though Trump reopened the possibility of pursuing the fund this week. The settlement also established audit protections for Trump, his family members and companies. Last month, a judge extended a block on the “anti-weaponization” fund.
Cornyn and Tillis have also said they want limits on the audit protections.
A Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on whether to advance Blanche out of committee was postponed last week after it became clear that Blanche did not have enough Republican support. The committee vote on sending Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate has been rescheduled for Tuesday.
Trump suggested Saturday that he could keep Blanche as acting attorney general and push for the passage of an “anti-weaponization” bill if Cornyn and Tillis hold up the nomination. The president declared that the controversial fund would “immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done.” Just a day earlier, Trump had said that the fund was “dead” but added, “I wish it weren’t.”
Asked whether he would support an “anti-weaponization” fund bill, Kennedy said he would have to read it first.
“We already have an anti-weaponization fund, a pool of money that you can access if you’re abused by government, through the Federal Torts Claim Act,” he said, referring to a law that allows people to file claims against the federal government. “But if he wants to improve it, I’m willing to look at it. But I’m not going to give him a blank check.”
Asked whether anyone who attacked law enforcement or stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6 should be able to receive taxpayer money from the fund, Kennedy said he would “take them off the table.”
“It’s too emotional of an issue, and it’s too important of an issue,” he said.
The senator noted that Jan. 6 defendants who believe they were wronged by the federal government can already file claims, which could be evaluated by a judge through an existing law.
Kennedy previously said that he believed Blanche when the acting attorney general told lawmakers the Justice Department was not pursuing the “anti-weaponization” fund anymore.
“I think the attorney general is a man of his word, and I’m very comfortable with what he told us, that there would not be an anti-weaponization fund,” Kennedy said in June.
